blocks.content: Writing an API that works is easy. Writing one that's clean, consistent, and scales with your team is the real skill. REST API design is a set of conventions not laws that make your API predictable for any developer who uses it.

blocks.alt: A REST API that also communicates clearly is what separates working code from good design

blocks.content: A well-designed REST API should feel intuitive almost predictable. Developers shouldn’t need to rely on documentation for every action; instead, they should be able to infer endpoints naturally from consistent patterns.
For example, if someone wants to fetch all comments on post 5, they should be able to confidently guess:

This kind of clarity comes from thoughtful, uniform design across the API. When naming conventions, resource structures, and HTTP methods are applied consistently, the API becomes self-explanatory reducing friction, speeding up development, and minimizing errors.
In short, great APIs don’t just work they communicate.
The most common mistake: putting verbs in URLs. REST URLs should identify resources (nouns), not actions (verbs). The HTTP method is the verb don't repeat it in the path.
Good APIs are structured around resources like: users, orders, products

["GET /users → retrieve all users","GET /users/42 → retrieve a specific user","POST /orders → create a new order","DELETE /orders/9 → delete an order","GET /users/42/orders → retrieve all orders for a user"]

blocks.content: When a resource belongs to another resource, nest the URL to express that ownership clearly. Keep nesting to 2 levels max deeper gets messy.
It shows how APIs structure URLs to represent relationships between resources (like users → orders, posts → comments).

blocks.alt: Nesting a URL expresses ownership between resources, like an order belonging to a user

blocks.content: Nesting makes ownership clear (e.g., an order belongs to a user), but should be limited to 2 levels to keep endpoints simple.
Each method has a specific meaning. Using the wrong method breaks the contract and causes bugs (like caching a POST response, or losing data on a GET).

blocks.alt: The HTTP method carries the verb, so the URL only ever needs to name the resource

blocks.content:

","POST/products→ Create resource, not idempotent (calling twice creates duplicates)
","PUT/products/5→ Replace entire resource, idempotent
","PATCH/products/5→ Update partial fields only (e.g., price)
","DELETE/products/5→ Remove resource, idempotent
"]

DELETE/products/5→ Remove resource, idempotent

blocks.content: HTTP methods definewhat action you're performing on a resource, and using them correctly ensures predictable, bug-free APIs.
Each method has rules (like GET = read only, POST = create, PUT/PATCH = update, DELETE = remove) and violating them can break caching, idempotency, or data consistency.
Replace the full resource. You must send all fields every time. If any field is missing, it may get overwritten (e.g., set to null). Idempotent (same request → same result).
Update specific fields only. You send only the fields you want to change. Other fields remain unchanged.

blocks.alt: A specific status code tells the client what happened before it even reads the response body

blocks.content: Returning 200 for everything even errors is one of the biggest REST API sins. The status code tells the client what happened before they even parse the body.

1. 200: OK → GET or PATCH succeeded, response contains the resource
  2. 201: Created → POST succeeded, new resource created and returned
  3. 204: No Content → DELETE succeeded, no response body
  4. 400: Bad Request → Validation failed, missing/invalid fields
  5. 401: Unauthorized → No valid authentication token provided
  6. 403: Forbidden → Authenticated but not allowed (insufficient permissions)
  7. 404: Not Found → Resource with given ID does not exist
  8. 409: Conflict → Duplicate or conflicting data (e.g., email already exists)
  9. 422: Unprocessable Entity → Valid JSON but business rule failed
  10. 429: Too Many Requests → Rate limit exceeded
  11. 500: Internal Server Error → Server crashed or unexpected failure

blocks.alt: URL versioning is the easiest to test and debug, which is why most real-world APIs use it

blocks.content: APIs evolve. If you change a response shape without versioning, you break every client using your API. Version your API from day one even if you only have v1 for years.
Here the version is part of the URL itself.
This makes it very easy to see which version you are using, even directly in the browser. It’s simple to test, debug, and maintain. That’s why most real-world APIs use this approach.
Here the version is sent in the request header instead of the URL. The URL looks clean, but the version is hidden.
Because of that, it’s harder to test and debug, especially in a browser, since you can’t easily set headers there.
Here the version is passed as a query parameter. It’s easy to implement and test, but not considered a strong standard. Over time it can make APIs messy, so it’s used less often.
Never return an unlimited list. If your GET /products returns all 2 million products at once, you'll crash the server and the client. Always paginate collections.
Here, instead of asking for page numbers, you ask for data after a specific point (cursor).
The cursor is usually an encoded value (like last item’s id).
You get 20 items, and anextCursor. To get the next set, you pass that cursor again.
This is stable  even if new data is added, results don’t shift or break.
Here, you request data using page number and limit.
You directly jump to page 3 and get 10 items. Easy to understand and implement.
Problem: If new items are added, pages shift → you may see duplicates or miss data.

blocks.alt: Filtering, sorting, and searching are all handled through query parameters on the same endpoint

blocks.content: Use query parameters for all of these never create separate endpoints for each filter combination.

These are query parameters used to control what data you get from an API. Filtering narrows results, sorting orders them, and search finds matching records. You can combine all for precise and efficient queries.
→ returns shipped orders for user 42 in 2024
→ returns products sorted by newest first
→ search + sort by price (low to high) + paginated results
Most APIs need to know who is making the request. The standard approach today is Bearer tokens passed in the Authorization header, not in the URL.
Send tokens in request headers to keep them secure. URLs can get logged, cached, and stored in browser history, exposing sensitive data.

["Tokens in URLs (/orders?token=abc123) get stored in browser history, server logs, proxies, and analytics tools. Anyone with access to these can steal the token.Why headers are good (secure)
","Authorization: Bearer abc123is sent in HTTP headers, not stored in URLs. It’s less exposed, not cached by default, and safer for sensitive data like tokens.
"]
